question: Where do I find a fractional CRO in Charleston?
body:
## Direct Answer
You find a fractional CRO in Charleston through three main channels: fractional-executive marketplaces and staffing firms that vet part-time revenue leaders, warm referrals from the local founder and investor community, and direct outreach to operators already advising Lowcountry companies. The fastest reliable path is a referral from a Charleston VC, angel group, or a founder who has already used one, because a fractional Chief Revenue Officer engagement lives or dies on trust and context-fit, not on a job board.

Charleston's tech and services economy has matured enough that fractional revenue leadership is a real, available option here — not something you have to import blind from Atlanta or Austin. This guide walks through exactly where to look, how to tell a genuine operator from a repackaged consultant, what a Charleston engagement typically costs and covers, and how to structure the first ninety days so the hire actually moves pipeline instead of just producing slide decks.

## What is a fractional CRO and why would a Charleston company hire one?
A fractional Chief Revenue Officer is an experienced revenue executive who owns your go-to-market strategy and revenue number on a part-time, ongoing basis — usually one to three days a week — instead of a full-time salaried seat. They sit above your sales, marketing, and customer-success functions, align them around a single revenue motion, and are accountable for the outcome. Unlike a consultant who diagnoses and leaves, a fractional CRO stays embedded, hires and coaches your reps, sits in your pipeline reviews, and carries the number alongside you.

For a Charleston company, the appeal is specific. Many of the region's fastest-growing firms — software startups clustered around the Charleston Digital Corridor, logistics and port-adjacent services, healthcare and hospitality tech, and professional-services rollups — hit a familiar wall around one to ten million in revenue. The founder has been the de facto head of sales, a couple of reps are closing on instinct, and there is no repeatable system. A full-time CRO at that stage can cost three hundred thousand dollars-plus in total compensation before you know whether the role is even needed. A fractional CRO gives you that senior judgment at a fraction of the cost and risk, and buys you the twelve to eighteen months of clarity you need before committing to a full-time hire. If you want the deeper economic argument, PULSE covers it in [the fractional-versus-full-time cost breakdown](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/fractional-cro-cost).

The other reason is timing. Charleston's talent pool for senior GTM leadership is real but thin compared to a coastal tech hub. A great full-time CRO may not want to relocate to the Lowcountry for an unproven Series A. A fractional operator, often already local or remote-friendly, will take the engagement precisely because it is part-time and portfolio-shaped. You get access to talent that would otherwise be out of reach.

## Where do I actually find one in Charleston — the channels ranked?
There are five channels, and they are not equal. Ranked by signal quality for a Charleston search:

**1. Warm referrals from the local ecosystem.** This is the highest-signal source and where you should start. Charleston's founder network is small and connected. Ask your investors, your board, other founders in your Slack and peer groups, and the organizations that convene them: the Charleston Digital Corridor, the Harbor Accelerator / Harbor Entrepreneur Center, and local angel groups. A name that comes back with a specific story — "she took our pipeline from chaos to a real forecast in a quarter" — is worth ten cold marketplace profiles.

**2. Fractional-executive marketplaces and networks.** National platforms now curate vetted fractional CROs and will filter for Southeast or remote-friendly operators. These are useful when your local network comes up empty or you want to interview a wider slate quickly. Treat the platform's vetting as a floor, not a guarantee — you still run your own diligence.

**3. Boutique RevOps and sales-consulting firms with fractional practices.** Some regional advisory firms staff fractional revenue leaders as a service line. The upside is a bench and a methodology behind the individual; the risk is you get a junior "associate" doing the work while a partner's name is on the SOW.

**4. LinkedIn direct outreach.** Search titles like "Fractional CRO," "Fractional VP Sales," and "Revenue Advisor" filtered to the Charleston metro and the broader Southeast. Look at who is already posting substantively about revenue operations, not just anyone with the title in their headline.

**5. Executive-search / staffing firms.** Traditional recruiters can source fractional talent but are built for full-time placement economics; expect this to be the slowest and most expensive channel, best reserved for when the others fail.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A[Need identified] --> B{Do you have local referrals}
  B -->|Yes| C[Warm intros from investors and founders]
  B -->|No| D[Fractional marketplaces and networks]
  C --> E[Shortlist of two to four operators]
  D --> E
  E --> F[Structured interviews and reference checks]
  F --> G{Fit confirmed}
  G -->|Yes| H[Ninety day paid trial engagement]
  G -->|No| E
  H --> I[Extend or convert to full time]
```

Work the channels in parallel, but weight your energy toward referrals. The goal of the first pass is a shortlist of two to four people you would genuinely trust with the number — not a spreadsheet of thirty profiles.

## How do I vet a fractional CRO so I don't hire a slide-deck consultant?
The single biggest failure mode is hiring someone who advises instead of operates. A real fractional CRO leaves fingerprints on your CRM, your comp plan, and your reps' behavior. A repackaged consultant leaves a strategy document. Vet for operator DNA.

Ask for specific, recent, hands-on outcomes: "Walk me through the last pipeline you personally rebuilt. What was the forecast accuracy before and after? How many reps did you hire or coach out? What did you change in the CRM?" Vague answers about "aligning stakeholders" and "driving synergies" are a red flag. You want stage-definition changes, a specific dashboard they built, a comp plan they redesigned, a deal they personally unstuck.

Check that they can operate at your stage. A CRO who scaled a company from fifty to two hundred million may be lost — and bored — inside a two-million-dollar Charleston startup that needs someone to build the first real sales process from scratch. Stage-fit matters more than logo prestige. PULSE goes deep on this in [the fractional-CRO vetting scorecard](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/fractional-cro-vetting).

Reference-check like you mean it. Talk to at least two founders who worked with them, and ask the disconfirming question directly: "What did they get wrong, and would you hire them again?" Silence or spin on that question tells you everything.

Finally, confirm bandwidth and portfolio honesty. A fractional CRO carrying six clients cannot give any of them real attention. Ask how many active engagements they hold, how many days a week you actually get, and how they handle a fire drill when two clients need them the same morning. Two to four concurrent clients is healthy; eight is a warning sign.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Candidate] --> B[Operator proof]
  A --> C[Stage fit]
  A --> D[References]
  A --> E[Bandwidth]
  B --> F{Green on all four}
  C --> F
  D --> F
  E --> F
  F -->|Yes| G[Advance to trial]
  F -->|No| H[Pass]
```

If a candidate is green on operator proof, stage fit, references, and bandwidth, they earn a paid trial. If any one of those is red, keep looking — the Charleston market is deep enough that you do not have to settle.

## What does a fractional CRO cost in Charleston, and how are engagements structured?
Pricing for fractional revenue leadership is set by the market rather than by geography, so a Charleston engagement is priced similarly to one anywhere in the Southeast — the operator's experience, your stage, and the day-count drive the number far more than the zip code. Engagements are almost always structured as a monthly retainer tied to a committed number of days or a defined scope, not hourly billing.

Common structures you will encounter:

- **Retainer for a fixed cadence** — e.g., "two days a week for six months." Predictable and the most common shape. You are buying ongoing ownership.
- **Scope-based project plus ongoing retainer** — a heavier first ninety days to build the revenue system, then a lighter maintenance cadence. This front-loads the value.
- **Retainer plus performance component** — a base monthly fee with an upside tied to pipeline or revenue milestones. This aligns incentives but requires clean attribution and mutual trust, so it usually comes later in a relationship, not on day one.

Rather than anchor on a number that would be guesswork for your specific situation, get two or three quotes from your shortlist and compare the day-rate and scope side by side. Be wary of the extremes: a rate far below market usually means an inexperienced operator or someone spread across too many clients, while a premium rate is only worth it if the references prove outsized outcomes at your stage. PULSE maintains a working framework for pricing these engagements in [the fractional revenue leadership pricing guide](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/fractional-revenue-pricing).

Whatever the structure, insist on three things in the agreement: a clear scope of what they own, a short initial term with an exit ramp (a ninety-day trial before a longer commitment), and defined success metrics you both signed off on before day one. A fractional CRO who resists a trial period or won't commit to measurable outcomes is telling you how the engagement will go.

## How do I structure the first ninety days so the hire actually works?
The first ninety days determine whether a fractional CRO becomes indispensable or becomes overhead. Structure them deliberately.

**Days 1 to 30 — diagnose and stabilize.** The operator should be in your CRM, your call recordings, and your pipeline reviews within the first week. Their job this month is to find the truth: where deals actually stall, whether your forecast is fiction, which reps are coachable, and where the biggest leak in the funnel sits. Expect a clear, unsentimental diagnosis at the end of month one — not a hundred-page deck, but a short list of the two or three things that matter most.

**Days 31 to 60 — build the system.** Now they install repeatable process: defined pipeline stages with exit criteria, a real forecast cadence, a cleaned-up comp plan if needed, and the dashboards you will run the business on going forward. This is where the operator-versus-consultant distinction shows up hardest — a real fractional CRO builds the machine and trains your team to run it, rather than becoming a dependency. For the mechanics of the operating system they should be installing, see [the RevOps foundation playbook](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/revops-foundation-playbook).

**Days 61 to 90 — prove it moves the number.** By the end of the quarter you want evidence in the metrics: tighter forecast accuracy, faster stage progression, a cleaner pipeline, reps executing a defined motion. This is your decision point — extend the engagement, expand it, convert toward full-time, or part ways.

Set the success metrics before day one and review them at each thirty-day mark. Give the fractional CRO genuine authority over the revenue org for the engagement — a part-time leader with no mandate cannot change rep behavior — while keeping the founder close enough to unblock decisions fast. The engagements that fail usually fail because the founder either abdicates entirely or refuses to let go at all. The right posture is partnership: they own the revenue system, you own the company.

## Related questions
### How is a fractional CRO different from a sales consultant?
A consultant diagnoses and hands you recommendations; a fractional CRO embeds part-time, owns the revenue number, hires and coaches reps, and stays accountable for outcomes over months, not a one-time report.

### Can a fractional CRO work remotely for a Charleston company?
Yes. Most fractional CROs work hybrid or remote with periodic on-site visits. Prioritize operator quality and stage-fit over physical proximity, though a local or Southeast-based operator eases in-person team building.

### When should a Charleston startup hire a fractional CRO instead of a VP of Sales?
Hire a fractional CRO when you need senior strategy and system-building across sales, marketing, and success but can't yet justify a full-time executive — typically in the one-to-ten-million revenue band where the motion is still unproven.

### How long do fractional CRO engagements usually last?
Most run six to eighteen months. Many start with a ninety-day trial, extend into an ongoing retainer, and either wind down once the system is self-sustaining or convert toward a full-time hire the fractional leader helps recruit.

### What size company benefits most from a fractional CRO?
Companies roughly between one and twenty million in revenue benefit most — large enough to have a real revenue team and budget, small enough that a full-time CRO would be premature or unaffordable.

## FAQ
**How much does a fractional CRO cost?**
It's priced as a monthly retainer tied to a committed number of days per week and the operator's experience, not hourly or by geography. Get two or three quotes from your shortlist and compare day-rate against scope; be skeptical of rates far below or far above the market range your candidates converge on.

**Where is the best place to start looking in Charleston?**
Warm referrals from local investors, founders, and organizations like the Charleston Digital Corridor and Harbor Entrepreneur Center. Referrals carry the trust and context-fit that a fractional revenue engagement depends on, and they outperform cold marketplace searches.

**Do I need a full-time CRO eventually, or is fractional enough?**
It depends on scale. Many companies run fractional indefinitely if the model works; others use a fractional CRO to build the system and prove the role's value, then convert to full-time — often with the fractional leader helping recruit their own replacement.

**What's the biggest risk when hiring a fractional CRO?**
Hiring an advisor who produces strategy decks instead of an operator who changes rep behavior and pipeline reality. Vet hard for hands-on, recent, stage-appropriate outcomes and check references with the disconfirming question.

**How many clients does a good fractional CRO carry at once?**
Typically two to four concurrent engagements. That range lets them give each client real attention. Six or more is a warning sign that you won't get the bandwidth you're paying for — ask directly and confirm the days you're promised.

**Should the engagement include a trial period?**
Yes. Structure a ninety-day paid trial with defined success metrics before committing to a longer term. An operator who resists a trial or won't commit to measurable outcomes is signaling how the whole engagement will go.

**Can a fractional CRO hire and manage my sales team?**
Yes — that's core to the role. A real fractional CRO interviews and hires reps, coaches the ones who are coachable, transitions out the ones who aren't, and installs the management cadence, rather than just advising from the sidelines.

**What should I have ready before the first interview?**
Your current revenue numbers, pipeline data, comp plans, org chart, and an honest statement of the problem you're trying to solve. The better a candidate can interrogate your real situation in the first conversation, the more it tells you about how they'll operate.
